title: Buying a Field in a Doomed Land
summary: With Babylon's army at the walls and Jeremiah under arrest in the palace guardhouse, the LORD tells him to buy his cousin's family field at Anathoth, land already under enemy occupation. Jeremiah pays, has the deed signed, sealed, witnessed, and stored in a clay jar, and then prays, puzzled, to the God for whom nothing is too hard. God answers that the city will certainly fall for its long idolatry, but that he will gather his people again, make an everlasting covenant with them, and fields will once more be bought and sold in this land.
story: The Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33) now moves from poetry to a dated event, and the timing is the point. Chapters 30 and 31 promised restoration in soaring language; chapter 32 shows Jeremiah staking his own money on it at the darkest possible moment. The chapter holds judgment and hope together more tightly than any other in the book. Jerusalem's fall, told in chapters 37 to 39 and 52, is only months away, and Jeremiah has been imprisoned for saying so. Yet the same prophet signs a deed for the future, and God's answer repeats both halves: the city will burn, and the land will be bought again.
historical:
Verse 1 dates the episode to the tenth year of Zedekiah and the eighteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, about 588 or 587 BC. The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem had begun in Zedekiah's ninth year (52:4) and would end with the city's fall in his eleventh. At one point an Egyptian army's approach forced the Babylonians to lift the siege briefly (37:5-11). Jeremiah had been confined in the courtyard of the guard, a place of detention within the palace complex, after being arrested as a suspected deserter (37:11-21). Anathoth, his home town, lay about three miles northeast of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, already in Babylonian hands.

This chapter introduces Baruch son of Neriah by name, Jeremiah's scribe and companion, who will write down his prophecies in chapter 36. A clay seal impression bearing the name of Berechiah (the long form of Baruch) son of Neriah the scribe appeared on the antiquities market in the 1970s and was widely published as his, but because it did not come from a controlled excavation some scholars have questioned whether it is genuine.
cultural:
Israel's law kept family land within the family. If a man fell into poverty and had to sell his land, his nearest relative had the right and duty to buy it back, to redeem it, so that it would not pass out of the clan (Leviticus 25:25; compare Boaz in Ruth 4). Hanamel, perhaps needing silver in the famine of the siege, offers Jeremiah that right. Seventeen shekels was a weight of silver, roughly seven ounces, since coinage was not yet in general use in Judah; silver was weighed on scales for each transaction.

The legal procedure in verses 10 to 14 matches practice known from ancient documents. A contract was written twice on one sheet; one copy was rolled and sealed so that it could not be altered, and the other left open for reference. Double documents of this kind are known from Jewish papyri found at Elephantine in Egypt, from the fifth century BC. Storing documents in sealed clay jars protected them from damp and decay; the Dead Sea Scrolls, found in jars in caves near Qumran, survived for about two thousand years this way.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 15 are a narrative, with a flashback in verses 3 to 5 explaining why Jeremiah was imprisoned, and the purchase told in careful legal detail so the reader feels its seriousness. Verses 16 to 25 are Jeremiah's prayer, which rehearses God's power in creation and in the exodus, admits that judgment has come just as God said, and ends in bewilderment: why buy a field now? Verses 26 to 44 are God's answer, which picks up Jeremiah's own words (“Nothing is too difficult for You” in verse 17 becomes “Is anything too difficult for Me?” in verse 27) and moves from judgment (28 to 35) to restoration (36 to 44). The final verse returns to the purchase: fields will be bought, deeds signed and sealed, in the very places Jeremiah named.

outline.t: The purchase of the field at Anathoth
Jeremiah's prayer: nothing is too hard for you
God's answer: the city will fall for its idolatry
An everlasting covenant; fields will be bought again

doctrines.note: Jeremiah acts on God's word before he understands it, then brings his confusion to God in prayer. Faith here is obedience that puts something real at stake on God's promise while the evidence points the other way.

Verse 40 calls the coming covenant everlasting and says God will put his fear in their hearts so they will never turn away. Like the new covenant of 31:31-34, it promises that God will secure both sides of the relationship.

Verses 29 to 35 name the specific sins that brought judgment: incense to Baal on rooftops, abominations in the temple, and children sacrificed to Molech in the Valley of Hinnom. Idolatry is not an abstract offense; it destroyed families and corrupted worship.

Jeremiah's prayer lists God's power, loyal love, justice, wisdom, and all-seeing eye (verses 17 to 19). The question “Is anything too difficult for Me?” echoes God's words to Abraham and Sarah about the promised son (Genesis 18:14).

words.note: Ge'ullah, redemption, the right or duty of a near relative (the go'el) to buy back family land or free a family member. It is the same family of words used of God as Israel's Redeemer. Jeremiah's purchase is an act of kinship redemption that becomes a sign of God's redemption of the land.
Qanah, to buy or acquire. It occurs nine times in the chapter, pressing home the ordinary commercial reality of what Jeremiah did. Buying land assumes there will be a future in which it can be used.

Pala, to be wonderful, extraordinary, or too difficult. The word links Jeremiah's confession in verse 17 with God's question in verse 27 and with Genesis 18:14. What is beyond human possibility is not beyond God.

christ: The link to Christ runs through the idea of the kinsman-redeemer. In Israel's law the nearest relative bought back what had been lost; the New Testament presents Christ as the one who redeems his people at a cost, not with silver but with his own blood (1 Peter 1:18-19). That connection is thematic rather than drawn from this chapter by any New Testament writer. The everlasting covenant of verse 40, with God putting his fear in his people's hearts so that they never turn away, belongs with the new covenant of chapter 31, which Jesus claimed to establish at the Last Supper. And the question of verse 27 recurs at the start of the Gospel story, when the angel tells Mary that nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37), echoing the same promise to Sarah.

hard.q: Verse 35 speaks of child sacrifice to Molech. Did Judah really do this, and what does God mean that it never entered his mind?
hard.a: The Old Testament repeatedly charges Judah and its neighbors with making children pass through the fire, and it names kings who did so: Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6). Scholars debate some details, such as whether Molech was the name of a god or a technical term for a kind of sacrifice, and whether every reference means killing a child or sometimes a dedication rite. But Jeremiah's words, with their mention of burning sons and daughters (7:31; 19:5), point to real sacrifice, and child sacrifice is attested in the wider ancient world. The phrase that it never entered God's mind does not mean God was ignorant of it. It is an idiom of total rejection: this was so far from anything God desired or commanded that it could never be connected with him. The verse is a pointed answer to anyone who thought such offerings could please the God of Israel.

questions: Jeremiah bought land he might never use, in a country about to be conquered. What would it look like for you to invest in a future you may not see?
Jeremiah obeyed first and asked his questions afterward in prayer. Is it harder for you to obey without understanding, or to bring your confusion honestly to God?
God says he will rejoice in doing his people good with all his heart and soul (verse 41). How does that picture of God compare with the one you usually carry?
